lead: 6LoWPAN lets IPv6 run on tiny IEEE 802.15.4 frames. 802.15.4 gives about 127 bytes per frame, too small for a normal IPv6 packet. 6LoWPAN sits between IPv6 and 802.15.4, compresses headers and splits big packets into fragments. RPL then chooses paths through the same low-power, lossy mesh. Together they let thousands of small sensors join an IP network without a gateway that translates every message. You meet them in smart meters, building sensors and industrial monitoring.
prereq: You need Chapter 3.2 for 802.15.4 frames and Chapter 3.1 for the network layer idea.

sections.h3: Constrained links and the two jobs

blocks.text: An IoT sensor node often has a small battery, a weak radio and links that drop packets. IEEE 802.15.4 gives it a frame with a 127-byte PHY payload, far below the 1280-byte minimum MTU that IPv6 expects. MTU means maximum transmission unit, the largest packet a link can carry. Two jobs follow. The first is adaptation: make IPv6 fit the small frame. 6LoWPAN does that. The second is routing: find a path from a node to a border router through a lossy mesh. RPL does that. A border router connects the mesh to the Internet. In RPL's tree view the root sits at rank 0, routers at rank 1, and end devices deeper. Rank is a node's position in the tree as measured by the objective function, often hop count. 6LoWPAN stands for IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Networks. It is an adaptation layer, not a routing protocol. RPL is a routing protocol, not an adaptation layer. Keep the two separate in an answer.

6LoWPAN sits between IPv6 and IEEE 802.15.4. Its main jobs are header compression, fragmentation and local mesh forwarding. Header compression uses IPHC, IPv6 Header Compression. A full IPv6 header is 40 bytes and a UDP header is 8 bytes. Many fields repeat or can be inferred: the version is 6, the prefix is known, and link-local addresses share a prefix. IPHC sends one dispatch byte and a set of bit flags saying which fields are omitted or compressed, plus the few fields that actually change; the receiver rebuilds the full 40-byte IPv6 header from those flags. This cuts overhead from dozens of bytes to a few bytes.

Fragmentation handles a packet larger than one frame. An IPv6 host may send up to 1280 bytes, but one 802.15.4 frame carries about 100 usable bytes. 6LoWPAN splits the IPv6 datagram. The first fragment carries a dispatch value, the datagram size and a tag. Later fragments carry the same tag and an offset. The destination reassembles them. More fragments mean more chances to lose one, and one lost fragment loses the whole datagram.

blocks.where: N_frag is the number of 6LoWPAN fragments; L_packet is the IPv6 datagram size in bytes; L_usable is the usable bytes per 802.15.4 frame after MAC and 6LoWPAN overhead; ceil rounds up to the next whole number.

blocks.text: Mesh-under and route-over are two ways to forward. In mesh-under, 802.15.4 MAC forwarding carries frames through a mesh; all nodes appear on one IP link. In route-over, every hop is an IP router; each 802.15.4 node forwards IPv6 packets. Route-over fits IP tools better; mesh-under saves IP header processing. Neighbor discovery is also adapted: IPv6 ND uses multicast and large options, so 6LoWPAN-ND compresses messages and registers addresses with a border router.

RPL is the IPv6 Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks. It builds a DODAG: Destination Oriented Directed Acyclic Graph. The DODAG has one root, often the border router, at rank 0. Each node picks a parent that is closer to the root, so rank increases as you move away. The objective function is the rule for choosing a parent and a path. It may use hop count, link quality or energy. RPL control messages are DIO (DODAG Information Object), DAO (Destination Advertisement Object) and DIS (DODAG Information Solicitation). The trickle timer controls DIO sending. When the network is stable, DIOs are rare. When a node hears inconsistent information, trickle speeds up. Upward routes go from a node to the root. Downward routes go from the root to nodes; nodes send DAO messages to advertise their prefixes. RPL suits many-to-one traffic, such as meters sending readings to a collector. Alternatives exist. LOADng is a lightweight on-demand protocol. AODV is a reactive protocol from mobile ad hoc networks. Use RPL when you need a stable tree and low control overhead.

spec.aria: A frame bar split into 25 bytes of overhead and 102 usable bytes; below, a 1,280-byte packet cut into 12 pieces of 102 bytes and a short 13th piece of 56 bytes.

examples.question: A 1280-byte IPv6 packet is sent over IEEE 802.15.4 frames. Each frame has a 127-byte PHY payload and 25 bytes of 6LoWPAN and MAC overhead. How many 6LoWPAN fragments are needed?
steps: List the frame payload: L_PHY = 127 bytes.
Subtract the overhead: L_usable = 127 − 25 = 102 bytes per frame.
Divide the IPv6 packet by usable bytes: 1280 ÷ 102 = 12.549... (12.55 when rounded to two decimals).
Round up because a partial fragment still needs a frame: ceil(12.549...) = 13 fragments.
examples.check:
import math
phy = 127
overhead = 25
usable = phy - overhead
packet = 1280
raw = packet / usable
frags = math.ceil(raw)
print(phy)
print(overhead)
print(usable)
print(packet)
print(round(raw, 2))
print(frags)

traps: 6LoWPAN is an adaptation layer, not a routing protocol. RPL routes; it does not compress IPv6 headers.
Fragmentation is not free: each extra fragment adds header bytes and increases the chance that the whole IPv6 packet is lost.
Rank is not an IP address or a hardware priority. It is the node's position in the DODAG under the objective function.
Mesh-under forwards at the MAC or adaptation layer on one IP link; route-over forwards IPv6 at every hop. Do not mix the two.
RPL is designed for low-power and lossy links, not for high-speed data centres.

quiz.a: IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Networks. It is an adaptation layer between IPv6 and IEEE 802.15.4.
IPv6 expects a minimum MTU of 1280 bytes, but an 802.15.4 frame has a 127-byte PHY payload, so a large IPv6 packet must be split and reassembled.

quiz.q: A 600-byte IPv6 packet uses frames with 120 usable bytes. How many fragments are needed?
A 6LoWPAN mesh loses many fragments. What happens to RPL's view of the link?
quiz.a: The link looks lossy, so its cost in the objective function rises. RPL may then move the node to a higher rank (further from the root in cost terms) or switch it to a different parent with better link quality; retransmissions add delay and control overhead.

quiz.q: What are the root and rank in an RPL DODAG?
quiz.a: The root is the single destination node at rank 0, often the border router. Rank measures a node's position away from the root under the objective function.

quiz.q: The root has rank 0. Node A has rank 1. Node B is a child of A under a hop-count objective function. What rank does B get?
quiz.a: Rank 2, because it is one more hop from the root.

quiz.q: Why does RPL use a trickle timer for DIO messages?
quiz.a: It keeps DIO traffic low when the tree is stable and increases updates when a node detects inconsistency, saving energy without slow recovery.

quiz.q: Name two routing protocols used as alternatives to RPL in low-power networks.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, 6LoWPAN and RPL appear in smart metering, building automation and industrial sensor meshes, often under the Thread stack. Newer work combines header compression with LPWAN technologies and with SCHC, a compression scheme for constrained links. Researchers tune RPL objective functions for energy, latency and reliability. Search for '6LoWPAN IPHC', 'RPL objective function' and 'Trickle timer' to go deeper.
